cards.definition: **Definition.** The set or type from which every object and quantified variable is drawn and under which operations and relations are interpreted.
major_error_concepts: Treating an untyped symbol as though its admissible values were obvious.
cards.prompt: Define Ambient mathematical domain. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The set or type from which every object and quantified variable is drawn and under which operations and relations are interpreted.

cards.definition: **Definition.** For an implication P implies Q, the converse is Q implies P, the inverse is not P implies not Q, and the contrapositive is not Q implies not P. Only the contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original implication in general.
major_error_concepts: Calling the converse equivalent because it uses the same words.
cards.prompt: Distinguish the converse, inverse, and contrapositive of P implies Q. Which one is logically equivalent to the original implication?
required_concepts: The converse of P implies Q is Q implies P.
The inverse is not P implies not Q.
The contrapositive is not Q implies not P and is logically equivalent to the original implication.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A definition stipulates the meaning of a term by declaring its objects, conditions, and resulting property or construction; it is unfolded in reasoning rather than proved as a theorem.
major_error_concepts: Trying to prove a definition or citing the term without its decisive clause.
cards.prompt: Define Definition clause. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A definition stipulates meaning through declared objects, conditions, and a resulting property or construction.
A definition is unfolded in reasoning rather than proved as a theorem.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The closed claim that at least one domain element satisfies a predicate with a witness or justified nonconstructive existence obligation.
major_error_concepts: Giving an object without checking every required property.
cards.prompt: Define Existential quantification. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The closed claim that at least one domain element satisfies a predicate with a witness or justified nonconstructive existence obligation.

cards.definition: **Definition.** To establish exists x in D, P(x), one must identify or validly obtain a witness w in D and establish P(w); when eliminating a proved existential, the temporary witness must be arbitrary apart from the stated property.
major_error_concepts: Naming an object without proving it lies in the domain and satisfies the predicate, or assuming an existential witness has an unstated special property.
cards.prompt: Define Existential witness choice. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Existential introduction requires a witness w in the declared domain D.
The witness must satisfy the predicate P(w).
Existential elimination may use only the properties stated for its arbitrary temporary witness.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A variable occurrence is free when it is not governed by a binder and bound when it lies within the scope of a quantifier or other local binder.
major_error_concepts: Letting a bound variable escape its scope or silently capturing a free variable.
cards.prompt: Define Free and bound variables. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A free variable occurrence is not governed by a binder.
A bound variable occurrence lies within the scope of a quantifier or other local binder.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The connective true when at least one component is true including the case both are true unless exclusivity is stated.
major_error_concepts: Reading mathematical or as exclusive without an explicit condition.
cards.prompt: Define Inclusive logical disjunction. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The connective true when at least one component is true including the case both are true unless exclusivity is stated.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The biconditional P if and only if Q is true exactly when P and Q have the same truth value; proving it requires both P implies Q and Q implies P.
major_error_concepts: Proving only one direction and writing iff.
cards.prompt: Define Logical biconditional. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: P if and only if Q is true exactly when P and Q have the same truth value.
A proof must establish both P implies Q and Q implies P.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The connective true exactly when both component propositions are true.
major_error_concepts: Treating and as a sequencing word that does not require both claims.
cards.prompt: Define Logical conjunction. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The connective true exactly when both component propositions are true.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Propositions P and Q are logically equivalent when they have the same truth value under every admissible interpretation, written P equivalent-to Q; equivalently, the biconditional P iff Q is logically valid.
major_error_concepts: Calling two propositions logically equivalent because they agree on one assignment or because both happen to be true in the current situation.
cards.prompt: Define Logical equivalence. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: P and Q have the same truth value under every admissible interpretation.
Equivalently, P iff Q is logically valid.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The connective producing a proposition true exactly when the governed proposition is false with scope fixed by parentheses.
major_error_concepts: Negating only the nearest word while losing the governed expression.
cards.prompt: Define Logical negation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The connective producing a proposition true exactly when the governed proposition is false with scope fixed by parentheses.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The material implication P implies Q is false exactly when P is true and Q is false; in every other truth assignment it is true.
major_error_concepts: Treating implication as causal explanation or as its converse.
cards.prompt: Define Material implication. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: P implies Q is false exactly when P is true and Q is false.
It is true in every other truth assignment.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A mathematical object is distinct from the notation or representation used to denote it; two expressions denote the same object only under a stated equality or equivalence criterion.
major_error_concepts: Calling visually similar notation the same object without an equality rule.
cards.prompt: Define Mathematical object identity. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: An object is distinct from the notation or representation used to denote it.
Two expressions denote the same object only under a stated equality or equivalence criterion.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The directional reading in which P is sufficient for Q and Q is necessary for P exactly when P implies Q.
major_error_concepts: Reversing necessary and sufficient because the conclusion appears second.
cards.prompt: Define Necessary and sufficient conditions. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The directional reading in which P is sufficient for Q and Q is necessary for P exactly when P implies Q.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The dependency-sensitive sequence of universal and existential binders whose exchange can change witness ownership and truth.
major_error_concepts: Swapping quantifiers because the same variables and predicate remain visible.
cards.prompt: Define Nested quantifier order. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The dependency-sensitive sequence of universal and existential binders whose exchange can change witness ownership and truth.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A property-valued expression whose truth depends on one or more free inputs from declared domains.
major_error_concepts: Assigning one truth value to an open predicate without an input or quantifier.
cards.prompt: Define Predicate on a domain. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A property-valued expression whose truth depends on one or more free inputs from declared domains.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A closed declarative mathematical sentence that is true or false under its specified interpretation.
major_error_concepts: Calling a command question or open formula a proposition.
cards.prompt: Define Proposition with truth value. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A closed declarative mathematical sentence that is true or false under its specified interpretation.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The recursive transformation exchanging universal with existential and negating the governed predicate while preserving domain and binder order.
major_error_concepts: Negating a quantified claim while keeping the same quantifier, or changing its domain, produces a different statement rather than its logical negation.
cards.prompt: Define Quantified-statement negation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The recursive transformation exchanging universal with existential and negating the governed predicate while preserving domain and binder order.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A definition stipulates meaning, a conjecture is proposed but unproved, and a theorem is a proved proposition; within a conditional theorem, its hypotheses are the assumed conditions and its conclusion is the claim those conditions imply.
major_error_concepts: Calling a conjecture a theorem, or treating a theorem's conclusion as an assumption rather than the claim supported by its hypotheses.
cards.prompt: How do a definition, conjecture, theorem, hypothesis, and conclusion differ?
required_concepts: A definition stipulates meaning, a conjecture is unproved, and a theorem is a proved proposition.
Hypotheses are the assumed conditions of a conditional statement.
The conclusion is the claim asserted under those hypotheses.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The specified interpretation of atomic propositions from which compound truth values are computed by connective rules.
major_error_concepts: Inferring truth from the English plausibility of the sentence instead of connective semantics.
cards.prompt: Define Truth assignment and semantic evaluation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The specified interpretation of atomic propositions from which compound truth values are computed by connective rules.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The conjunction of existence and the assertion that any two satisfying objects are equal under the specified equality relation.
major_error_concepts: Showing one convenient witness and calling it unique.
cards.prompt: Define Unique existence quantification. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The conjunction of existence and the assertion that any two satisfying objects are equal under the specified equality relation.

cards.definition: **Definition.** From a proved universal statement forall x in D, P(x), universal instantiation permits P(t) for any declared term t in D.
major_error_concepts: Instantiating a universal statement with an object not known to belong to its quantified domain.
cards.prompt: Define Universal instantiation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The premise is a proved statement forall x in D, P(x).
The chosen term t must be known to lie in D.
The permitted conclusion is P(t).

cards.definition: **Definition.** The closed claim that a predicate holds for every element of a declared domain with an arbitrary-element proof obligation.
major_error_concepts: Checking several values and declaring the universal statement proved.
cards.prompt: Define Universal quantification. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The closed claim that a predicate holds for every element of a declared domain with an arbitrary-element proof obligation.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The explicit separation between facts temporarily available and the exact want-to-show that terminates the argument.
major_error_concepts: Listing the theorem again without exposing the local assumption and goal.
cards.prompt: Define Assumption and proof goal. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The explicit separation between facts temporarily available and the exact want-to-show that terminates the argument.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The separate proof that every admissible object lies in at least one specified case with overlap allowed unless disjointness is needed.
major_error_concepts: Calling positive and negative exhaustive while omitting zero.
cards.prompt: Define Case exhaustiveness certificate. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The separate proof that every admissible object lies in at least one specified case with overlap allowed unless disjointness is needed.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The invalid dependency in which the target or an equivalent unproved claim is used to derive itself.
major_error_concepts: Calling a long dependency cycle a proof because every sentence is true conditionally.
cards.prompt: What is wrong with using the target claim, or an equivalent unproved claim, to derive itself?
required_concepts: The argument uses the target, or an equivalent unproved claim, as support for itself.
The dependency therefore supplies no independent route from accepted premises to the target.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The method giving an explicit witness then verifying every property in the existential predicate.
major_error_concepts: Naming an object without verifying every property in the existential predicate does not establish that it is a witness.
cards.prompt: Define Constructive existence proof. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The method giving an explicit witness then verifying every property in the existential predicate.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The method that assumes the exact negation of the specified claim and derives an impossibility whose dependency discharges that assumption.
major_error_concepts: Deriving an unrelated false equation that does not depend on the negated target.
cards.prompt: Define Contradiction proof architecture. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The method that assumes the exact negation of the specified claim and derives an impossibility whose dependency discharges that assumption.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The method proving P implies Q by directly proving not Q implies not P under their logical equivalence.
major_error_concepts: Proving Q implies P establishes the converse, not the contrapositive of P implies Q.
cards.prompt: Define Contrapositive proof architecture. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The method proving P implies Q by directly proving not Q implies not P under their logical equivalence.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The architecture that replaces a named property by its exact defining clauses and reconstructs the target definition after valid transformations.
major_error_concepts: Citing oddness repeatedly without introducing the existential integers.
cards.prompt: Define Definition-unfolding proof. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The architecture that replaces a named property by its exact defining clauses and reconstructs the target definition after valid transformations.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The method for a conditional or universal claim that starts from arbitrary admissible objects and hypotheses and derives the stated conclusion.
major_error_concepts: Starting from the conclusion and manipulating it without reversible steps.
cards.prompt: Define Direct proof architecture. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The method for a conditional or universal claim that starts from arbitrary admissible objects and hypotheses and derives the stated conclusion.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The sequence of separately justified biconditionals connecting several conditions with every link preserving both directions.
major_error_concepts: Using a chain of one-way implications and writing equivalence signs.
cards.prompt: Define Equivalence-chain proof. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The sequence of separately justified biconditionals connecting several conditions with every link preserving both directions.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The planning distinction between deriving consequences from premises and analyzing what sufficient subgoals would establish the target without treating backward heuristics as proof steps.
major_error_concepts: Writing the desired conclusion first and assuming every reversed implication is valid.
cards.prompt: Distinguish forward from backward proof search. Why is backward search not itself a proof step?
required_concepts: Forward search derives consequences from the available premises.
Backward search identifies sufficient subgoals that would establish the target.
Backward search is a planning heuristic, not permission to reverse an implication as a proof step.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The requirement to prove P implies Q and Q implies P under the same specified domains and definitions.
major_error_concepts: Writing two examples one for each truth value instead of two universal implications.
cards.prompt: Define If-and-only-if proof architecture. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The requirement to prove P implies Q and Q implies P under the same specified domains and definitions.

cards.definition: **Definition.** An argument establishing that some witness must exist without identifying one while preserving the exact existential conclusion.
major_error_concepts: Claiming nonconstructive existence supplies an algorithm or canonical witness.
cards.prompt: Define Nonconstructive existence proof. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: An argument establishing that some witness must exist without identifying one while preserving the exact existential conclusion.

cards.definition: A proof by cases chooses conditions whose union covers every admissible possibility, then proves the desired conclusion under each condition. The cases may overlap; disjointness is not required. Exhaustiveness is essential, including boundary or equality cases when applicable.
major_error_concepts: A proof by cases is invalid whenever its cases overlap, even if they cover all possibilities and each establishes the conclusion.
cards.prompt: What makes a proof-by-cases argument complete, and must its cases be disjoint?
required_concepts: Every admissible possibility belongs to at least one case.
Establish the conclusion in every case.
Overlapping cases are allowed; uncovered cases are not.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A truth-preserving argument form such as modus ponens that licenses a conclusion from premises of exact matching form.
major_error_concepts: Using affirming the consequent from Q and P implies Q to infer P.
cards.prompt: Define Rule of inference. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A truth-preserving argument form such as modus ponens that licenses a conclusion from premises of exact matching form.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The method assuming two arbitrary satisfying objects and deriving their equality after existence has been handled separately.
major_error_concepts: Showing one candidate works and stopping.
cards.prompt: Define Uniqueness proof architecture. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The method assuming two arbitrary satisfying objects and deriving their equality after existence has been handled separately.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The refutation of a universally quantified claim by one admissible object for which its predicate fails.
major_error_concepts: Giving an object outside the domain or one that still satisfies the claim.
cards.prompt: What claim does Universal disproof by counterexample refute, and why?
required_concepts: The refutation of a universally quantified claim by one admissible object for which its predicate fails.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The valid proof of P implies Q obtained because P is impossible on the specified domain without asserting Q independently.
major_error_concepts: Calling the conclusion universally true or pretending an impossible witness exists.
cards.prompt: Define Vacuous conditional proof. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The valid proof of P implies Q obtained because P is impossible on the specified domain without asserting Q independently.

cards.definition: An argument is logically valid if no interpretation makes all its premises true while its conclusion is false: the conclusion follows from the premises. Validity concerns the inference, not whether the premises are actually true. An argument is sound when it is valid and its premises are true in the intended interpretation; mathematical proofs work relative to explicitly accepted axioms and hypotheses.
major_error_concepts: Any argument with a false premise is logically invalid, regardless of its inference form.
cards.prompt: Distinguish logical validity from soundness in a mathematical argument.
required_concepts: Validity rules out true premises with a false conclusion.
A valid argument can have a false premise.
Soundness additionally requires true premises in the intended interpretation.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The set containing exactly objects belonging to both sets.
major_error_concepts: Returning all elements from either set.
cards.prompt: Define Binary intersection. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The set containing exactly objects belonging to both sets.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The set containing exactly objects belonging to at least one of two sets.
major_error_concepts: Counting common elements twice or reading union as pair formation.
cards.prompt: Define Binary union. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The set containing exactly objects belonging to at least one of two sets.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The set of ambient elements not in A whose value is undefined until a universe is specified.
major_error_concepts: Taking an absolute complement without a universal set.
cards.prompt: Define Complement relative to a universe. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The set of ambient elements not in A whose value is undefined until a universe is specified.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The set-equality architecture proving A subset B and B subset A by separate arbitrary-element arguments.
major_error_concepts: Showing one inclusion and invoking visual obviousness for the reverse.
cards.prompt: Define Double-containment equality proof. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The set-equality architecture proving A subset B and B subset A by separate arbitrary-element arguments.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The proof of containment or equality by choosing an arbitrary element translating membership through definitions and deriving target membership.
major_error_concepts: Drawing a diagram and omitting the arbitrary-element argument.
cards.prompt: Define Element-chasing proof pattern. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The proof of containment or equality by choosing an arbitrary element translating membership through definitions and deriving target membership.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The unique set with no elements and the declared ambient set relative to which complements and unrestricted variables are interpreted.
major_error_concepts: Calling the empty set an element of every set or changing the universal set silently.
cards.prompt: Define Empty and universal sets. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The unique set with no elements and the declared ambient set relative to which complements and unrestricted variables are interpreted.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It moves complementation through arbitrary indexed unions or intersections while reversing the set operation, supporting elementwise set proofs; the universe and index family must remain fixed and explicit.
major_error_concepts: Applying finite notation without binding the index or complement universe.
cards.prompt: What is Indexed De Morgan law used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It moves complementation through arbitrary indexed unions or intersections while reversing the set operation, supporting elementwise set proofs
the universe and index family must remain fixed and explicit.

cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** For a family (A_i) indexed by I inside one universe U, the complement of the union over I equals the intersection over I of the complements, and the complement of the intersection equals the union of the complements.
major_error_concepts: Applying finite notation without binding the index or complement universe.
cards.prompt: State Indexed De Morgan law, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
required_concepts: The family is indexed by one set I and all complements are relative to one universe U.
The complement of the union over I is the intersection over I of the complements.
The complement of the intersection over I is the union over I of the complements.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A function-like assignment i maps to A_i over a declared index set allowing repeated member sets.
major_error_concepts: Treating an indexed family as an ordinary set and losing index multiplicity or order.
cards.prompt: Define Indexed family of sets. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A function-like assignment i maps to A_i over a declared index set allowing repeated member sets.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The set of elements belonging to every A_i for all i in I corresponding to universal membership over the index domain.
major_error_concepts: Using one convenient index as sufficient for intersection membership.
cards.prompt: Define Indexed intersection. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The set of elements belonging to every A_i for all i in I corresponding to universal membership over the index domain.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The set of elements belonging to at least one A_i for an index i in I corresponding to existential membership over the index domain.
major_error_concepts: Requiring an element to belong to every indexed set.
cards.prompt: Define Indexed union. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The set of elements belonging to at least one A_i for an index i in I corresponding to existential membership over the index domain.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The order-sensitive pair construction and set A times B of all pairs with first coordinate in A and second in B.
major_error_concepts: Swapping coordinates or replacing the product by a union.
cards.prompt: Define Ordered pair and Cartesian product. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The order-sensitive pair construction and set A times B of all pairs with first coordinate in A and second in B.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The property that every two sets with distinct indices have empty intersection which is stronger than the sets merely being distinct.
major_error_concepts: Checking only that the displayed sets are unequal.
cards.prompt: Define Pairwise-disjoint family. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The property that every two sets with distinct indices have empty intersection which is stronger than the sets merely being distinct.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The set of all subsets of A whose elements are themselves sets and whose finite size is two to the size of A.
major_error_concepts: Listing a and b directly as power-set elements.
cards.prompt: Define Power-set construction. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The set of all subsets of A whose elements are themselves sets and whose finite size is two to the size of A.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The set of all elements from a declared domain satisfying a predicate with variable scope and admissibility explicit.
major_error_concepts: Using set-builder notation without declaring the ambient domain, or treating two descriptions with the same elements as different sets.
cards.prompt: Define Set-builder construction. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The set of all elements from a declared domain satisfying a predicate with variable scope and admissibility explicit.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The relative-complement construction A minus B containing elements of A not in B and generally not symmetric.
major_error_concepts: Treating A minus B and B minus A as equal.
cards.prompt: Define Set difference. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The relative-complement construction A minus B containing elements of A not in B and generally not symmetric.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The equality principle that two sets are equal exactly when they have the same elements regardless of order or repetition in notation.
major_error_concepts: Treating display order or repeated listings as set identity.
cards.prompt: Define Set extensionality. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The equality principle that two sets are equal exactly when they have the same elements regardless of order or repetition in notation.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The proposition x belongs to A relating an object to a set and distinct from subset containment.
major_error_concepts: Replacing an element by its singleton or using membership between two arbitrary sets as containment.
cards.prompt: Define Set membership. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The proposition x belongs to A relating an object to a set and distinct from subset containment.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The universal containment A subset B separated from strict containment A proper subset B requiring inequality.
major_error_concepts: Using one shared element as proof of subset containment.
cards.prompt: Define Subset and proper-subset distinction. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The universal containment A subset B separated from strict containment A proper subset B requiring inequality.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The set of elements in exactly one of A and B equal to their union minus their intersection.
major_error_concepts: Including the shared element or confusing it with ordinary difference.
cards.prompt: Define Symmetric difference. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The set of elements in exactly one of A and B equal to their union minus their intersection.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The conjunction of injectivity and surjectivity giving exactly one preimage for each codomain element.
major_error_concepts: Proving only one mapping property.
cards.prompt: Define Bijective function. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The conjunction of injectivity and surjectivity giving exactly one preimage for each codomain element.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The same assignment with codomain narrowed to a set containing the range which can change surjectivity but not outputs.
major_error_concepts: Choosing a codomain that omits an attained output.
cards.prompt: Define Corestriction of a function. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The same assignment with codomain narrowed to a set containing the range which can change surjectivity but not outputs.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The separation among allowed inputs declared output space and actually attained output subset.
major_error_concepts: Calling the range the codomain or inferring surjectivity from output existence.
cards.prompt: Define Domain codomain and range distinction. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The separation among allowed inputs declared output space and actually attained output subset.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The equality requiring the same domain codomain and equal output on every input under the specified convention.
major_error_concepts: Comparing formulas only and ignoring domain or codomain.
cards.prompt: Define Equality of functions. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The equality requiring the same domain codomain and equal output on every input under the specified convention.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The design of a typed assignment followed separately by totality output-membership and requested mapping-property proofs.
major_error_concepts: Giving a correspondence picture without a total rule or proof.
cards.prompt: Define Explicit function construction. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The design of a typed assignment followed separately by totality output-membership and requested mapping-property proofs.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The total single-valued assignment sending each domain element to exactly one codomain element.
major_error_concepts: Treating any formula as a total function on every apparent input.
cards.prompt: Define Function as typed assignment. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The total single-valued assignment sending each domain element to exactly one codomain element.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The typed map id_A from A to A sending each element to itself and serving as the neutral element for composition.
major_error_concepts: Using one untyped identity across incompatible domains.
cards.prompt: Define Identity function. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The typed map id_A from A to A sending each element to itself and serving as the neutral element for composition.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The codomain subset f[A] of outputs attained by inputs from A with existential witness membership.
major_error_concepts: Applying f to the set symbol as if it were one input.
cards.prompt: Define Image of a subset. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The codomain subset f[A] of outputs attained by inputs from A with existential witness membership.

cards.definition: **Definition.** For any function f, images preserve arbitrary unions exactly, while f[A intersection B] is contained in f[A] intersection f[B]; equality for every pair A,B holds when f is injective on the relevant domain.
major_error_concepts: Assuming images preserve every set operation as equality.
cards.prompt: Define Image preservation laws. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Images preserve arbitrary unions exactly.
The image of an intersection is contained in the intersection of the images.
Injectivity on the relevant domain upgrades the intersection inclusion to equality.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The property that equal outputs force equal inputs equivalently distinct inputs have distinct outputs.
major_error_concepts: Checking only that every input has an output.
cards.prompt: Define Injective function. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The property that equal outputs force equal inputs equivalently distinct inputs have distinct outputs.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The typed map f inverse:B to A satisfying both compositions as identities exactly when f is bijective.
major_error_concepts: Taking a symbolic reciprocal or ignoring the codomain restriction.
cards.prompt: Define Inverse function. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The typed map f inverse:B to A satisfying both compositions as identities exactly when f is bijective.

cards.definition: **Definition.** For f:A->B and g:B->A, g composed f=id_A makes g a left inverse and always forces f to be injective. Conversely, an injection admits a total left inverse when A is nonempty, by mapping points outside f(A) to a chosen element of A; the empty-domain case works only when B is also empty.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every injection from the empty set into a nonempty codomain has a total left inverse, or claiming a left inverse is automatically two-sided.
cards.prompt: Define Left inverse and injectivity. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A left inverse g satisfies g composed f=id_A and therefore f is injective.
If A is nonempty, an injection f:A->B admits a total left inverse after choosing one element of A for values outside f(A).
If A is empty, such a total left inverse exists only when B is empty.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The domain subset f inverse[B] of inputs whose outputs lie in B defined even when f has no inverse function.
major_error_concepts: Assuming preimage notation means a bijective inverse function.
cards.prompt: Define Preimage of a subset. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The domain subset f inverse[B] of inputs whose outputs lie in B defined even when f has no inverse function.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Preimages preserve arbitrary unions and intersections, as well as complements relative to the codomain and set differences, with equality and without requiring injectivity or surjectivity.
major_error_concepts: Adding an injectivity assumption or using inverse-function algebra.
cards.prompt: Define Preimage preservation laws. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Preimages preserve arbitrary unions and intersections exactly.
Preimages preserve codomain-relative complements and set differences exactly.
No injectivity or surjectivity assumption is required.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A function defined on equivalence classes whose output is unchanged when any equivalent representative replaces the chosen one.
major_error_concepts: Computing with one representative and assuming the class-level map is well defined.
cards.prompt: Define Representative-independent function. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A function defined on equivalence classes whose output is unchanged when any equivalent representative replaces the chosen one.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The function obtained by narrowing the domain while preserving outputs and using a compatible codomain.
major_error_concepts: Changing values while calling the result a restriction.
cards.prompt: Define Restriction of a function. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The function obtained by narrowing the domain while preserving outputs and using a compatible codomain.

cards.definition: **Definition.** For f:A->B and h:B->A, f composed h=id_B makes h a right inverse and always forces f to be surjective. Conversely, a surjection admits a right inverse exactly when one can choose one preimage in every fiber; this is automatic for finite B but is the Axiom-of-Choice principle for arbitrary families.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every arbitrary surjection has a right inverse in ZF without a chosen representative from each fiber, or claiming a right inverse implies injectivity.
cards.prompt: Define Right inverse and surjectivity. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A right inverse h satisfies f composed h=id_B and therefore f is surjective.
The converse requires selecting one preimage from every fiber f^{-1}({b}).
The selection is automatic for finite B but choice-sensitive for arbitrary families.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The property that every codomain element has at least one domain preimage.
major_error_concepts: Showing only that outputs lie in the codomain.
cards.prompt: Define Surjective function. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The property that every codomain element has at least one domain preimage.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The typed map g composed f applying f first then g when the output of f lies in the domain of g.
major_error_concepts: Reversing the application order or composing incompatible maps.
cards.prompt: Define Typed function composition. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The typed map g composed f applying f first then g when the output of f lies in the domain of g.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The representation gcd(a,b)=ax+by for integers x and y obtained constructively from Euclidean descent.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every integer linear combination equals the gcd.
cards.prompt: Define Bézout identity. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The representation gcd(a,b)=ax+by for integers x and y obtained constructively from Euclidean descent.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The proof that addition and multiplication of representatives respect congruence classes before quotient arithmetic is accepted.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying residue labels without a representative-independence proof.
cards.prompt: Define Congruence compatibility. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The proof that addition and multiplication of representatives respect congruence classes before quotient arithmetic is accepted.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The equivalence relation a congruent b mod n when n divides a-b for positive modulus n under the specified convention.
major_error_concepts: Comparing only last digits or using modulus zero.
cards.prompt: Define Congruence modulo an integer. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The equivalence relation a congruent b mod n when n divides a-b for positive modulus n under the specified convention.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The integer relation a divides b exactly when b=ak for some integer witness k.
major_error_concepts: Using decimal quotient intuition without an integer witness.
cards.prompt: Define Divisibility relation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The integer relation a divides b exactly when b=ak for some integer witness k.

cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** For integers a and b with b nonzero, there exist unique integers q and r such that a=bq+r and 0 is less than or equal to r, which is less than |b|.
major_error_concepts: Using truncation toward zero and returning a negative remainder.
cards.prompt: State the division theorem, including the condition on the divisor and the existence, uniqueness, and range of the quotient and remainder.
required_concepts: The dividend a and divisor b are integers with b nonzero.
There exist unique integers q and r satisfying a=bq+r.
The remainder satisfies 0 less than or equal to r less than |b|.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** The division theorem gives the unique quotient-remainder normal form behind modular arithmetic and Euclidean reduction; it does not justify a negative remainder under the stated convention.
major_error_concepts: Treating machine-language truncating division as the theorem's nonnegative-remainder convention for every sign of a and b.
cards.prompt: What is the division theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It supplies a unique quotient-remainder normal form for modular arithmetic and Euclidean reduction.
Its stated convention requires 0 less than or equal to r less than |b|, not a negative truncating remainder.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The bridge-course result that ordinary induction strong induction and well ordering can derive one another under a fixed natural-number foundation.
major_error_concepts: Calling the methods textually identical rather than logically interderivable.
cards.prompt: Define Equivalence of natural-number proof principles. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The bridge-course result that ordinary induction strong induction and well ordering can derive one another under a fixed natural-number foundation.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The repeated quotient-remainder descent preserving the gcd until a zero remainder and supporting Bezout back substitution.
major_error_concepts: Stopping at a nonzero remainder or losing quotient equations needed for reconstruction.
cards.prompt: Define Euclidean algorithm. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The repeated quotient-remainder descent preserving the gcd until a zero remainder and supporting Bezout back substitution.

cards.definition: **Definition.** For integers a and b not both zero, gcd(a,b) is the unique positive common divisor d such that every common divisor of a and b divides d.
major_error_concepts: Calling the largest displayed factor the gcd without the universal property.
cards.prompt: Define Greatest common divisor. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: d is a positive divisor of both a and b.
Every common divisor of a and b divides d.
The inputs are not both zero under this convention.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The complete finite set of initial cases required before the successor step covers the specified index domain.
major_error_concepts: Proving only one base and leaving an unreachable parity class.
cards.prompt: Define Induction base range. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The complete finite set of initial cases required before the successor step covers the specified index domain.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The disciplined separation between assuming P(k) for an arbitrary admissible k and proving P(k+1) without assuming the target.
major_error_concepts: Writing assume P(k+1) in the induction step.
cards.prompt: Define Induction hypothesis and step target. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The disciplined separation between assuming P(k) for an arbitrary admissible k and proving P(k+1) without assuming the target.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The proof by choosing the least failing natural index and using smaller valid cases to contradict its failure.
major_error_concepts: Choosing a counterexample without proving a least one exists.
cards.prompt: What are the preconditions and decisive move of the least-counterexample proof method?
required_concepts: Assume a counterexample exists in a well-ordered domain and choose a least one.
Use validity of all smaller cases to contradict failure at the least counterexample.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It proves a predicate for every natural index from a base by combining a genuine base case with a universally valid successor step; finite pattern checking is not a substitute for the implication.
major_error_concepts: Checking several values and calling the pattern proved.
cards.prompt: What is Ordinary induction principle used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It proves a predicate for every natural index from a base by combining a base case with a universally valid successor step.
Checking finitely many cases is not a substitute for proving the successor implication.

cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** Let n0 be a natural number and P(n) a proposition for every n at least n0. If P(n0) holds and, for every k at least n0, P(k) implies P(k+1), then P(n) holds for every n at least n0.
major_error_concepts: Checking several values and calling the pattern proved.
cards.prompt: State Ordinary induction principle, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
required_concepts: P(n0) holds for the declared natural-number base n0.
For every k at least n0, P(k) implies P(k+1).
Therefore P(n) holds for every n at least n0.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The base clauses and rule constructing later values from earlier governed values with existence and uniqueness separated from later property proofs.
major_error_concepts: Treating a recurrence without bases as a complete definition.
cards.prompt: Define Recursive definition. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The base clauses and rule constructing later values from earlier governed values with existence and uniqueness separated from later property proofs.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The finite dependency expansion that computes a specified input from base values without proving a universal property.
major_error_concepts: Using the desired closed form instead of the recursive definition being evaluated.
cards.prompt: Define Recursive function evaluation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The finite dependency expansion that computes a specified input from base values without proving a universal property.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A stronger predicate chosen because it carries information needed by the successor step while still implying the original target.
major_error_concepts: Repeating a failed weak induction without changing the missing invariant.
cards.prompt: Define Strengthened induction claim. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A stronger predicate chosen because it carries information needed by the successor step while still implying the original target.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It permits the full block of earlier cases as the induction hypothesis when one next case depends on several smaller instances, while remaining logically equivalent to ordinary induction; it never permits assuming the current or a larger case.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the theorem for n itself or for values not smaller.
cards.prompt: What is Strong induction principle used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It permits the full block of earlier cases when the next case depends on several smaller instances.
It is logically equivalent to ordinary induction over the natural numbers.
It never permits assuming the current case or a larger case.

cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** Let n0 be a natural number and P(n) a proposition for every n at least n0. If, for every n at least n0, the assumption that P(k) holds for all k from n0 through n-1 implies P(n), then P(n) holds for every n at least n0.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the theorem for n itself or for values not smaller.
cards.prompt: State Strong induction principle, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
required_concepts: For each n at least n0, the induction hypothesis may use P(k) for every k from n0 through n-1.
The block of earlier cases must imply P(n).
Therefore P(n) holds for every n at least n0.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The proof principle aligned to recursively generated objects with base constructors and one preservation case for each recursive constructor.
major_error_concepts: Inducting on an undefined size while omitting one constructor.
cards.prompt: Define Structural induction. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The proof principle aligned to recursively generated objects with base constructors and one preservation case for each recursive constructor.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Natural-number descent proves termination by assigning every state or recursive input a measure mu in N and proving that every allowed step strictly decreases mu. No infinite execution can then occur because N has no infinite strictly decreasing chain.
major_error_concepts: Claiming termination without specifying an N-valued measure, or without proving that every allowed step decreases it strictly.
cards.prompt: Define Well-founded descent. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Assign every state or recursive input a measure mu in N.
Prove that every allowed step strictly decreases mu.
There is no infinite strictly decreasing chain in N, so the process terminates.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It enables least-counterexample and minimal-obstruction proofs over the natural numbers and is equivalent in strength to induction there; ordinary integer or real order does not satisfy the same nonempty-subset guarantee.
major_error_concepts: Applying well ordering to integers or reals with their usual order without qualification.
cards.prompt: What is Well-ordering principle used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It enables least-counterexample and minimal-obstruction proofs over the natural numbers and is equivalent in strength to induction there
ordinary integer or real order does not satisfy the same nonempty-subset guarantee.

cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** Every nonempty subset of the natural numbers has a least element under the usual order.
major_error_concepts: Applying well ordering to integers or reals with their usual order without qualification.
cards.prompt: State Well-ordering principle, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
required_concepts: Every nonempty subset of the natural numbers has a least element under the usual order.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The requirement that xRy and yRx force x=y which permits one-way related distinct elements.
major_error_concepts: Reading antisymmetric as not symmetric or as no reverse pairs.
cards.prompt: Define Antisymmetric relation property. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The requirement that xRy and yRx force x=y which permits one-way related distinct elements.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The requirement that xRy implies not yRx which also forces irreflexivity.
major_error_concepts: Calling antisymmetry and asymmetry equivalent.
cards.prompt: Define Asymmetric relation property. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The requirement that xRy implies not yRx which also forces irreflexivity.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The subset R of A times B whose pair membership records when an A-object is related to a B-object.
major_error_concepts: Treating a relation as an untyped verbal comparison.
cards.prompt: Define Binary relation as ordered-pair set. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The subset R of A times B whose pair membership records when an A-object is related to a B-object.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The surjective map pi:A to A/R sending each element to its equivalence class.
major_error_concepts: Calling the projection injective when a class has multiple representatives.
cards.prompt: Define Canonical quotient projection. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The surjective map pi:A to A/R sending each element to its equivalence class.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It proves that equivalence classes form a partition and lets one replace any overlap between two classes by equality; partial overlap is impossible for classes of the same equivalence relation.
major_error_concepts: Calling overlapping equivalence classes merely partially overlapping.
cards.prompt: What is Class equality-or-disjointness theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It proves that equivalence classes form a partition and lets one replace any overlap between two classes by equality
partial overlap is impossible for classes of the same equivalence relation.

cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** Let approximately be an equivalence relation on A. For any a,b in A, the classes [a] and [b] are equal exactly when a is equivalent to b; otherwise the two classes are disjoint.
major_error_concepts: Calling overlapping equivalence classes merely partially overlapping.
cards.prompt: State Class equality-or-disjointness theorem, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
required_concepts: The relation is one equivalence relation on a carrier A, with a and b in A.
The classes [a] and [b] are equal exactly when a is equivalent to b.
If a is not equivalent to b, the classes are disjoint.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The order-relative notions of comparable pairs totally ordered subsets and pairwise incomparable subsets.
major_error_concepts: Using numerical magnitude instead of the specified order relation.
cards.prompt: Define Comparability chains and antichains. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The order-relative notions of comparable pairs totally ordered subsets and pairwise incomparable subsets.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The subset [a] of all carrier elements equivalent to representative a with representative choice not part of class identity.
major_error_concepts: Treating [1] and [4] as different because their labels differ.
cards.prompt: Define Equivalence class. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The subset [a] of all carrier elements equivalent to representative a with representative choice not part of class identity.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** The correspondence permits switching between pairwise relation language and quotient-by-block language; it does not choose a canonical representative in any block.
major_error_concepts: Claiming that the correspondence chooses a distinguished or canonical representative from every equivalence class.
cards.prompt: What is the equivalence-partition correspondence used for, and what does it not supply?
required_concepts: It converts an equivalence relation into quotient blocks and a partition into a same-block relation.
It does not choose canonical representatives.

cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** For any set A, equivalence relations on A correspond exactly to partitions of A: the equivalence classes of a relation form a partition, and belonging to the same block of a partition defines an equivalence relation.
major_error_concepts: Calling an overlapping family a partition, or defining the same-block relation from blocks that do not cover A.
cards.prompt: State the equivalence-partition correspondence, including both constructions.
required_concepts: The equivalence classes of every equivalence relation on A form a partition of A.
For every partition of A, same-block membership defines an equivalence relation on A.
The two constructions recover the original relation or partition.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The construction map sends an equivalence relation to its collection of classes and sends a partition to the relation x~y iff x and y lie in the same block; composing the two maps recovers the original structure.
major_error_concepts: Giving only one construction or failing to check that applying the reverse construction recovers the original relation or partition.
cards.prompt: What are the two construction maps in the equivalence-partition correspondence?
required_concepts: Send an equivalence relation to the partition consisting of its equivalence classes.
Send a partition to the relation x~y iff x and y lie in the same block.
The two constructions recover the original relation or partition.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A reflexive symmetric transitive relation whose classes partition the carrier.
major_error_concepts: Checking only that examples have the same residue label.
cards.prompt: Define Equivalence relation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A reflexive symmetric transitive relation whose classes partition the carrier.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A finite order diagram is a representation of a finite poset that places larger elements above smaller ones and retains only cover relations, where y covers x iff x<y and no z satisfies x<z<y; equality, loops, and edges implied by transitivity are omitted.
major_error_concepts: Retaining every comparable pair as an edge and calling the result a Hasse-style order diagram.
cards.prompt: Define Finite order diagram. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The representation is for a finite poset.
Larger elements are placed above smaller elements.
The element y covers x exactly when x<y and no z satisfies x<z<y.
Only cover relations are retained; loops and transitive edges are omitted.

cards.definition: **Definition.** For R subseteq A x B, R^{-1}={(b,a) in B x A:(a,b) in R}. For S subseteq B x C, this course writes S composed R={(a,c) in A x C: there exists b in B with (a,b) in R and (b,c) in S}.
major_error_concepts: Reversing the declared composition order, omitting the shared carrier B, or placing inverse pairs in A x B instead of B x A.
cards.prompt: Define Inverse and composition of relations. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: R^{-1}={(b,a) in B x A:(a,b) in R} for R subseteq A x B.
For S subseteq B x C, (a,c) is in S composed R exactly when some b in B satisfies (a,b) in R and (b,c) in S.
The carriers and composition order are part of the definition.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The universal requirement that no carrier element relates to itself.
major_error_concepts: Calling a nonreflexive relation irreflexive after finding one failed diagonal.
cards.prompt: Define Irreflexive relation property. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The universal requirement that no carrier element relates to itself.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The quantified distinction between no strictly smaller or larger element and an element below or above every member of the subset.
major_error_concepts: Calling every minimal element least or every maximal element greatest.
cards.prompt: Define Minimal maximal least and greatest elements. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The quantified distinction between no strictly smaller or larger element and an element below or above every member of the subset.
cards.term: Minimal maximal least and greatest elements

cards.definition: **Definition.** A family of nonempty pairwise-disjoint blocks whose union is the carrier.
major_error_concepts: Listing overlapping subsets or omitting carrier coverage.
cards.prompt: Define Partition of a set. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A family of nonempty pairwise-disjoint blocks whose union is the carrier.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The distinction that a preorder is reflexive and transitive while a partial order additionally requires antisymmetry.
major_error_concepts: Calling every transitive relation an order.
cards.prompt: Define Preorder and partial order. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The distinction that a preorder is reflexive and transitive while a partial order additionally requires antisymmetry.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The set A modulo R whose elements are equivalence classes rather than representatives.
major_error_concepts: Writing quotient elements as raw integers without class semantics.
cards.prompt: Define Quotient set. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The set A modulo R whose elements are equivalence classes rather than representatives.

cards.definition: **Definition.** For a relation R on A, its reflexive closure is R union Delta_A, where Delta_A={(a,a):a in A}; it is the least reflexive relation on A containing R.
major_error_concepts: Adding arbitrary off-diagonal pairs or omitting a diagonal pair while claiming the least reflexive superrelation.
cards.prompt: Define Reflexive closure. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The construction is R union Delta_A with Delta_A={(a,a):a in A}.
It contains R and is reflexive on A.
It is contained in every reflexive relation on A that contains R.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The universal requirement xRx for every carrier element.
major_error_concepts: Checking one diagonal pair or confusing reflexive with symmetric.
cards.prompt: Define Reflexive relation property. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The universal requirement xRx for every carrier element.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A partial order may leave distinct elements incomparable; a total order is a partial order in which every pair x,y is comparable, so x<=y or y<=x.
major_error_concepts: Inferring totality from reflexivity, antisymmetry, and transitivity without checking comparability of every pair.
cards.prompt: How does a total order strengthen a partial order?
required_concepts: A partial order may contain incomparable distinct elements.
A total order is a partial order satisfying x<=y or y<=x for every pair x,y.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A strict partial order is irreflexive and transitive, while a non-strict partial order is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive; each determines the other by x<y iff x<=y and x!=y, and x<=y iff x<y or x=y.
major_error_concepts: Calling a strict order reflexive, or dropping antisymmetry when converting a non-strict preorder into a partial order.
cards.prompt: How do strict and non-strict partial orders correspond?
required_concepts: A strict partial order is irreflexive and transitive.
A non-strict partial order is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive.
The two representations convert by adjoining or removing equality.

cards.definition: **Definition.** For a relation R on A, its symmetric closure is R union R^{-1}; it is the least symmetric relation on A containing R.
major_error_concepts: Reversing every pair but discarding the original pairs, or calling a larger arbitrary symmetric relation the least closure.
cards.prompt: Define Symmetric closure. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The construction is R union R^{-1}.
It contains R and is symmetric.
It is contained in every symmetric relation containing R.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The requirement that xRy always implies yRx.
major_error_concepts: Inferring symmetry from a symmetric-looking diagram with missing reverse edges.
cards.prompt: Define Symmetric relation property. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The requirement that xRy always implies yRx.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The transitive closure R^+ of a relation R is the union of its positive powers R, R^2, R^3, ...; it relates x to y exactly when a nonempty finite R-path leads from x to y, and it is the least transitive relation containing R.
major_error_concepts: Adding only length-two composites and assuming transitivity, or including all diagonal pairs while claiming the positive rather than reflexive-transitive closure.
cards.prompt: Define Transitive closure. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: R^+ is the union of R^n for integers n>=1.
It records nonempty finite R-path reachability.
It is the least transitive relation containing R.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The requirement that xRy and yRz imply xRz for all carrier triples.
major_error_concepts: Checking only adjacent pairs in one displayed chain.
cards.prompt: Define Transitive relation property. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The requirement that xRy and yRz imply xRz for all carrier triples.

cards.definition: **Definition.** For S subseteq a poset P, u in P is an upper bound of S when s<=u for every s in S, and l in P is a lower bound when l<=s for every s in S; a least upper bound is below every upper bound and a greatest lower bound is above every lower bound, when such elements exist.
major_error_concepts: Requiring a bound to belong to S, or calling any upper bound the least upper bound.
cards.prompt: How do upper bounds, lower bounds, least upper bounds, and greatest lower bounds differ?
required_concepts: An upper bound u satisfies s<=u for every s in S.
A lower bound l satisfies l<=s for every s in S.
A least upper bound is below every upper bound, and a greatest lower bound is above every lower bound.
A bound need not belong to S, and a least or greatest bound need not exist.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The representative-independence proof that an operation on classes yields the same output class under equivalent inputs.
major_error_concepts: Testing one representative pair and assuming class-level validity.
cards.prompt: Define Well-defined quotient operation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The representative-independence proof that an operation on classes yields the same output class under equivalent inputs.

cards.definition: Different binary strings need not denote different real numbers: 0.1000...=0.0111.... A diagonal real-number argument must handle that ambiguity for both the listed representations and its constructed output. One safe transfer from binary sequences b_n to [0,1] is the ternary encoding sum_{n≥1} 2b_n/3^n. It is injective: at the first differing index k, the leading difference 2/3^k exceeds the largest possible later cancellation 1/3^k. Thus uncountably many binary sequences give uncountably many distinct reals.
major_error_concepts: Once every listed real is written using a binary expansion not eventually all 1s, any bit-flipped diagonal string necessarily represents a different real.
cards.prompt: What binary-expansion ambiguity can spoil a naive real-number diagonal argument, and how can an injective encoding avoid it?
required_concepts: Binary strings can differ while representing the same dyadic real.
Canonical input representations alone do not guarantee a canonical diagonal output.
Give an ambiguity-safe construction, such as the injective ternary 0/2 encoding.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The construction flipping the nth coordinate of the nth listed infinite binary sequence to differ from every listed sequence.
major_error_concepts: Flipping a finite prefix or failing to prove the new sequence belongs to the target set.
cards.prompt: Define Binary-sequence diagonal argument. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The construction flipping the nth coordinate of the nth listed infinite binary sequence to differ from every listed sequence.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It proves that forming a power set strictly increases cardinality and blocks every proposed enumeration by diagonalization; the contradiction concerns a claimed surjection, not self-membership of the diagonal subset.
major_error_concepts: Calling D paradoxical or asking whether D belongs to itself rather than testing D=f(a).
cards.prompt: What is Cantor power-set theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It proves that forming a power set strictly increases cardinality and blocks every proposed enumeration by diagonalization
the contradiction concerns a claimed surjection, not self-membership of the diagonal subset.

cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** For every set A, no function from A onto its power set P(A) exists; hence |A|<|P(A)|. The diagonal subset {a in A : a is not in f(a)} defeats any proposed surjection f.
major_error_concepts: Calling D paradoxical or asking whether D belongs to itself rather than testing D=f(a).
cards.prompt: State Cantor power-set theorem, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
required_concepts: For every set A, no function from A onto P(A) exists.
Consequently |A| is strictly less than |P(A)|.
The diagonal subset {a in A : a is not in f(a)} is omitted by any proposed surjection f.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The relation that cardinality of A is no greater than cardinality of B witnessed by an injection from A into B with direction fixed.
major_error_concepts: Using a surjection in the wrong direction without proving the needed conversion.
cards.prompt: Define Cardinal comparison by injection. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The relation that cardinality of A is no greater than cardinality of B witnessed by an injection from A into B with direction fixed.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The declared use of countable as finite-or-bijective-with-naturals and countably infinite as bijective with naturals.
major_error_concepts: Using countable and countably infinite interchangeably after declaring the broader convention.
cards.prompt: Define Countable and countably-infinite conventions. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The declared use of countable as finite-or-bijective-with-naturals and countably infinite as bijective with naturals.

cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** Let (A_n)_{n in N} be sets and suppose explicit surjections e_n:N->A_n are supplied for every nonempty A_n. Then union_n A_n is at most countable, by diagonally enumerating pairs (n,k) and removing repetitions. From only the assertion that each A_n is countable, selecting all e_n uses countable choice.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a choice-free theorem from bare per-set countability while neither supplying a family of enumerations nor assuming countable choice.
cards.prompt: State the supplied-enumeration form of the countable-union theorem and its choice qualification.
required_concepts: The family is indexed by N and an explicit surjection e_n:N->A_n is supplied for each nonempty A_n.
A diagonal traversal of (n,k) enumerates the union, so the union is at most countable.
Obtaining all e_n from bare per-set countability is countable-choice sensitive.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** With enumerations supplied for a countable family, the theorem reduces the union to one diagonal traversal of a two-index array; bare per-set countability requires a choice principle to select all enumerations.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A surjective sequence e:N->A enumerates every element and certifies that A is at most countable; a bijection e:N->A certifies that A is countably infinite. Removing duplicates from a surjective enumeration yields a bijective enumeration only when A is known infinite.

A bijection N->A certifies exact countable infinity.
Duplicate removal gives a bijective enumeration only after A is known infinite.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A set is infinite when it is not finite, and Dedekind-infinite when it is bijective with a proper subset. In ZF, Dedekind-infinite implies infinite; the converse may fail, while the axiom of countable choice suffices for it.

Dedekind-infinite implies infinite in ZF.

cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** If there is an injection from A to B and an injection from B to A, then there is a bijection between A and B.

cards.definition: A set is uncountable when it is neither finite nor countably infinite. A sufficient obstruction is that no injection from it into N exists; for a nonempty set, showing that every proposed enumeration by N misses an element also suffices. Merely showing no bijection with N suffices only after establishing that the set is infinite. One failed candidate enumeration does not rule out all enumerations.
major_error_concepts: The singleton {0} is uncountable because there is no bijection N→{0}.
cards.prompt: What must an argument rule out to prove a set uncountable, and why is no bijection with N alone insufficient?
required_concepts: Uncountable excludes both finite and countably infinite sets.
The obstruction must apply to every possible enumeration or injection, not just one attempt.
No bijection with N requires an additional infinitude premise.
